items.author: secretsofuniverse
items.text:
🧬 Scientists have found that sperm cells can seem to sidestep one of Newton’s most famous laws.

Newton’s third law says that for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.

That works beautifully for ordinary objects.

But sperm cells live in a very different world.

They swim through thick, sticky fluids where inertia barely matters and viscous drag dominates almost everything.

To move, sperm use a thin tail called a flagellum, which bends in waves and pushes against the surrounding fluid.

A study by researchers at Kyoto University analyzed human sperm data and the swimming motion of the green alga Chlamydomonas.

They found that these tiny swimmers use a property called odd elasticity.

In normal elastic materials, a bend produces a matching response.

But in odd elastic systems, the response can be non-reciprocal. The internal motion does not simply push back in the usual equal-and-opposite way.

That lets flagella keep beating without losing as much energy to the fluid.

So sperm are not breaking physics.

They are exploiting a loophole of active matter, where living systems burn energy and operate far from equilibrium.

At the microscopic scale, even motion has its own strange rules.

📄 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Ishimoto et al., “Odd Elastohydrodynamics: Non-Reciprocal Living Material in a Viscous Fluid”, PRX Life (2023)

items.author: ryanhallyall
items.text:
A super El Niño is building in the Pacific. Here is how that can set up a massive snowstorm this winter.

The polar vortex is the swirl of cold air over the North Pole. When it is strong, the cold stays bottled up.

Strong El Niño winters send big waves of energy toward the pole that can weaken or even split it late in the winter. Arctic air spills south.

At the same time, El Niño strengthens the storm track across the South.

Cold air meets a moisture loaded storm. That is a major winter storm.

So when you hear El Niño means a warm winter, do not assume that means no big snowstorms.

The Euro remains aggressive with rain coverage (largely into Thursday), spitting out over 1" of rain in Rochester. The GFS, on the other hand, suggests it barely rains at all.

items.author: MeteorologistChristopherNunley
items.text:
GULF OF CALIFORNIA SYSTEM | SW MOISTURE🌀🌧️⛈️a small area of low pressure has developed over the southern Gulf of California, producing disorganized showers and thunderstorms. The system has only a 10% chance of becoming a tropical depression or storm before moving inland over Sonora on Tuesday, so significant tropical development is unlikely.

However, development is not the main story here. This disturbance contains a pocket of tropical moisture and energy that will be drawn northward into the Southwest as it moves inland and interacts with the larger-scale weather pattern. The Gulf of California and eastern Pacific are important moisture sources for the Southwest monsoon, and disturbances near the Gulf can help enhance northward moisture transport.

In fact, a strong Gulf moisture surge is already pushing northward into Arizona and New Mexico, while deep southerly flow continues to transport moisture out of northern Mexico. That moisture, combined with disturbances moving through the Southwest, will support multiple rounds of showers and thunderstorms this week across Arizona and New Mexico, and surrounding areas, with this system serving to enhance the monsoon surge further. Heavy rainfall will be the biggest concern, with localized flash flooding possible - especially around burn scars, normally dry washes and arroyos, slot canyons, low-water crossings and other flood-prone areas. 

So even if this Gulf of California low never earns a name, its moisture and associated energy can still play a role in enhancing an already active Southwest monsoon pattern this week🌀🌧️⛈️

Locally heavy rain will also occur in the Panhandles where abundant moisture could produce high rainfall rates. Farther east, some storms may generate more wind than rain. Dry lightning could ignite new fires in northwestern Oklahoma where vegetation remains highly susceptible to burning.

items.author: EdPiotrowskiWPDE
items.text:
TROPICAL UPDATE 
1 PM TUESDAY 9/15/2026

BOTTOM LINE: No threats to the U.S.

We are smack dab in the heart of hurricane season, yet it’s been 13 days (and counting) since we’ve had a named storm anywhere in the Atlantic. That’s pretty remarkable considering this is typically the busiest part of the season.

There are no named storms out there right now, but I am watching a broad, non-tropical area of low pressure spinning well southeast of Bermuda. Wind shear is too strong for development at the moment, but it could relax by the weekend, giving the system a chance to organize into a tropical depression.

Computer models remain split. Traditional, physics-based models show little chance of development, while newer AI models are much more aggressive, although they’ve bounced around quite a bit from run to run.

The system could meander over the central Atlantic for a while, but eventually a dip in the jet stream should pick it up and carry it northeast and away from the U.S.

For now, Bermuda is really the only land area that needs to keep a close eye on it.

Enjoy the quiet!

items.author: secretsofuniverse
items.text:
🪞 Astronomers have found the shiniest planet ever seen beyond our Solar System.

The world is called LTT 9779 b, and it lies more than 260 light-years away from Earth.

It is about the size of Neptune, but it orbits its star in just 19 hours.

That puts it so close to its sun that its dayside reaches around 2,000°C.

At those temperatures, ordinary clouds should not exist.

But observations from ESA’s Cheops space telescope showed something stunning: LTT 9779 b reflects about 80% of the light falling on it.

That makes it almost as reflective as Venus, the brightest planet in our own sky.

The likely reason is a sky filled with metallic clouds, made of silicates, the stuff found in sand and glass, mixed with metals such as titanium.

Those clouds may act like a shield, reflecting starlight away and helping the planet keep its atmosphere.

That matters because LTT 9779 b sits in the “hot Neptune desert,” a region where Neptune-sized planets are not expected to survive so close to their stars.

A planet that should have been stripped bare is still shining like a mirror.

📄 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Hoyer et al., “The extremely high albedo of LTT 9779 b revealed by CHEOPS”, Astronomy & Astrophysics (2023)

items.text:
🪐 In its final hours, the spacecraft did something it was never built to do. It turned its antenna toward Earth and kept transmitting new science all the way down, sending back data about Saturn's atmosphere until the very second the planet tore it apart. It was still working when it died.

On September 15, 2017, NASA deliberately destroyed the Cassini spacecraft by flying it straight into Saturn. After 13 years orbiting the planet, Cassini was almost out of fuel, and the team faced a problem. If they left it drifting, it might one day crash into Enceladus or Titan, two moons that could possibly harbour life. Contaminating them with Earth microbes hitchhiking on the spacecraft was unacceptable.

So they chose a controlled ending. They called it the Grand Finale. In its last five months, Cassini did something no mission had ever attempted, threading 22 times through the narrow 2,000-kilometre gap between Saturn and its rings, a region nobody had dared to fly through before.

Then came the final plunge. Cassini hit the upper atmosphere and began to tumble. Its thrusters fought to keep the antenna pointed at Earth, firing harder and harder, until they couldn't win anymore. The signal cut out. About 83 minutes later, that last transmission reached Earth, arriving from a spacecraft that had already been gone for over an hour.

EYES ON EASTERN PACIFIC🌀we may see a noticeable increase in eastern Pacific tropical activity during the final days of September and into early October!

The broader atmospheric setup is expected to become more supportive of rising air and organized thunderstorms near the Pacific coast of Mexico. Several large-scale tropical disturbances could overlap during this period, increasing the possibility that one or more organized systems emerge.

The ocean is also unusually warm - both at the surface and below it - which could help sustain a developing cyclone. Subsurface temperature departures surpass 3.5°C in parts of the eastern Pacific, meaning cooler water may be less likely to reach the surface as quickly beneath a storm.

Any potential track is highly uncertain. However, autumn weather systems moving across the West can occasionally steer eastern Pacific cyclones or their moisture northward. That creates several possibilities, including movement toward western Mexico or Baja California and, in some scenarios, an eventual surge of tropical into Arizona and New Mexico, and possibly southeastern California and Texas and Oklahoma. 

At this stage, this is a signal for a potentially favorable pattern - not a prediction that a particular hurricane will form or strike land. Details concerning development, strength, timing and movement will remain unclear until a defined disturbance emerges. It is simply a period worth watching as late September approaches🌀

🧠 A leukemia drug may help stop breast cancer from spreading to the brain — but the evidence is still early.

Researchers studied HER2-positive breast cancer, a subtype that can be especially dangerous when it metastasizes to the brain.

They focused on two enzymes called ABL1 and ABL2 kinases. These enzymes appear to help cancer cells build up HER2 protein on their surface, supporting growth and spread.

In mouse experiments, blocking ABL signaling with asciminib, a drug already approved for certain leukemia patients, reduced the ability of HER2-positive breast cancer cells to colonize the brain.

The treatment also improved survival in preclinical models.

This does not mean asciminib is ready to treat breast cancer patients.

Human trials are still needed to test safety, dose, and whether the same effect happens in people.

But it points to a possible new way to target breast cancer after it reaches the brain.

📃 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 McKernan et al., “ABL kinases regulate translation in HER2+ cells through Y-box-binding protein 1 to facilitate colonization of the brain”, Cell Reports (2022)

Slow-moving storms could produce locally heavy rain, particularly around the Idaho mountains, but coverage will be isolated in nature.

By the weekend, high pressure strengthens across most of the Northwest, bringing drier and warmer weather everywhere. items.author: secretsofuniverse
items.text:
🧬 Asteroid Ryugu now contains the full alphabet of DNA and RNA.

Scientists have detected all five canonical nucleobases in samples returned from Ryugu by Japan’s Hayabusa2 mission.

These are adenine, guanine, cytosine, thymine and uracil, the molecular letters used by life on Earth to build DNA and RNA.

This does not mean life existed on Ryugu.

It means that some of the key ingredients used by genetic molecules can form in space and survive inside ancient asteroid material.

That makes Ryugu incredibly valuable.

Unlike meteorites that fall through Earth’s atmosphere and touch soil, Ryugu’s samples were collected directly from the asteroid and sealed for return to Earth.

That helps scientists study asteroid chemistry with far less contamination.

The discovery also matches what researchers have found in samples from asteroid Bennu, where all five nucleobases were detected too.

Together, Ryugu and Bennu suggest that the chemistry behind DNA and RNA was not rare in the early Solar System.

Long before life began on Earth, asteroids may have been carrying the molecular letters life would later use to write its genetic code.

The rocks were not alive.

But they may have delivered part of life’s alphabet.

📄 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Koga et al., “A complete set of canonical nucleobases in the carbonaceous asteroid (162173) Ryugu”, Nature Astronomy (2026)

LOS ANGELES EARTHQUAKE UPDATE‼️over the weekend, 107 earthquakes were recorded across two areas of Southern California! 101 earthquakes near Lennox, Inglewood and Hawthorne. This activity is near the Newport-Inglewood Fault Zone. The strongest earthquake in this sequence was a magnitude 2.7 near Lennox early Saturday morning. And 6 earthquakes approximately 16 miles east-southeast of Avalon. This activity is near the offshore San Pedro Basin fault system. The strongest was a magnitude 3.3 early Saturday morning, preceded two minutes earlier by a magnitude 3.0.

Many people may not have felt these earthquakes because most were extremely small. Many of the Lennox-area earthquakes also originated roughly 10-15 miles underground, while the Avalon sequence occurred offshore and several miles beneath the seafloor. Shaking from small, deep or offshore earthquakes often weakens considerably before reaching populated areas.

These appear to be two separate sequences. Their proximity to mapped faults does not confirm that those specific faults produced the earthquakes, and swarms do not necessarily mean a larger earthquake is coming. The numbers and preliminary magnitudes may change as seismic data are reviewed‼️

🌅 Frequent cannabis users may start the day with higher levels of the body’s main stress hormone.

Researchers studied 39 adults who used cannabis frequently and 43 healthy controls.

Participants reported stress levels and collected saliva samples when they woke up, 30 minutes later, and in the evening across two weekdays.

The main focus was cortisol, a hormone involved in stress response, blood pressure, metabolism, and daily alertness.

Both groups showed a similar morning rise in cortisol after waking.

But frequent cannabis users had higher cortisol levels right at awakening.

Those higher waking cortisol levels were also linked with more cannabis-related problems.

This does not prove cannabis caused the change. People with higher stress biology may also be more likely to use cannabis frequently.

But the finding suggests regular cannabis use may be connected to changes in the body’s daily stress rhythm.

📃 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Donner et al., “Subjective Stress and Diurnal Salivary Cortisol in Adults with Frequent Cannabis Use”, Cannabis (2026)

items.author: secretsofuniverse
items.text:
🧲 It’s official: physicists have directly imaged a strange third class of magnetic order.

For a long time, scientists mostly sorted ordered magnets into two major families.

Ferromagnets are the familiar kind. Their tiny magnetic moments line up in the same direction, creating an overall magnetic field.

Antiferromagnets are different. Their moments point in opposite directions, cancelling each other out so the material has no net magnetization.

Now, researchers have confirmed a third class called altermagnetism.

In an altermagnet, the magnetic moments also point in opposite directions. But the atomic environment around each moment is rotated in a special way.

That small geometric twist changes everything.

It gives the material some of the speed and stability of an antiferromagnet, while also allowing useful electronic effects normally associated with ferromagnets.

Using X-ray microscopy, scientists imaged altermagnetic domains inside manganese telluride, a material once treated as a simple antiferromagnet.

They also showed that these domains can be controlled in microscopic devices.

That matters because altermagnets could help build faster, denser and more energy-efficient memory and spintronic technologies.

They may even provide new clues in the physics of superconductivity.

A hidden form of magnetism has finally stepped into view.

📄 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Amin et al., “Nanoscale imaging and control of altermagnetism in MnTe”, Nature (2024)

items.author: secretsofuniverse
items.text:
OpenAI says an internal AI system has produced a proof for the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, one of the famous Millennium Prize Problems.

The question asks whether smooth fluid motion can suddenly break down and form a singularity.

In OpenAI’s claimed solution, a fluid starts smoothly from rest, keeps finite energy, but develops unbounded velocity in finite time.

That would be historic.

But the scale of the effort is just as striking.

OpenAI says the Navier-Stokes run used about 10,000 concurrent AI agents working for 88 hours.

Those agents exchanged 2.7 million messages and generated around 130 billion output tokens.

Across all the major problems OpenAI tested, the system used 4.9 million messages and about 300 billion output tokens.

Then GPT-6 Astra spent another 17 hours formalizing and checking the proof in Lean.

In other words, this was not one AI calmly thinking like a lone mathematician.

It was a huge industrial swarm of machines attacking a frontier problem with computing power that almost no academic group could match.

That is where the controversy begins.

NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster and Anthropic researcher Levent Alpöge had been working on closely related fluid equations and had used OpenAI tools during their research.

Buckmaster worried that private, unfinished work shared inside Codex could somehow have helped OpenAI’s system.

OpenAI denies this and says Buckmaster’s Codex prompts could not have influenced the result.

For now, the proof still needs mathematical scrutiny.

But the bigger question is already here.

When AI companies can provide the tools, hear that researchers are close, and then throw millions of machine hours at the same problem, science enters a very different world.

📄 TECHNICAL PAPER
📌 OpenAI, “Finite Time Blowup for Navier-Stokes”, OpenAI (2026)

🧠 A common diabetes drug may be linked to a lower risk of dementia decades later.

Researchers analyzed long-term follow-up from the Diabetes Prevention Program and its outcomes study, which began in the late 1990s.

The study included 1,483 older adults who had originally been at high risk for type 2 diabetes.

Those randomized to metformin had, on average, about 15.5 years of total metformin exposure.

When cognitive outcomes were assessed between 2022 and 2024, metformin randomization was linked to 60% lower odds of dementia compared with placebo, and 62% lower odds compared with intensive lifestyle intervention.

Metformin was also linked to slightly better memory performance over time.

But the result needs caution. The overall distribution of cognitive impairment did not differ significantly, and there were few dementia cases.

This is not a reason to take metformin without medical advice.

📃 RESEARCH PREPRINT
📌 Wander et al., “Randomized metformin and cognitive outcomes in the Diabetes Prevention Program Outcomes Study”, medRxiv (2026)

items.text:
🌊 The detectors had only been switched on for a few days. Scientists were still running tests, fine-tuning the equipment, not officially looking for anything yet. Then, at a moment when nobody was really watching, a signal rolled in from a collision that had happened 1.3 billion years ago. The universe didn't wait for them to be ready.

On September 14, 2015, the two LIGO observatories, one in Washington state and one in Louisiana, picked up the first gravitational waves ever directly detected. The signal came from two black holes, roughly 36 and 29 times the mass of our Sun, spiraling together and merging into one. In the final fraction of a second, they released more energy than all the stars in the observable universe combined, all of it as ripples in space-time itself.

Those ripples had been traveling for 1.3 billion years before they washed over Earth and stretched the LIGO detectors by a fraction of the width of a proton. The whole event, captured as a rising "chirp," lasted about two-tenths of a second.

The signal was so clean that some team members initially suspected it was a fake test injection. It wasn't. It was real. Einstein had predicted this exactly a century earlier, and almost nobody thought we'd ever actually catch one.

🧬 An experimental compound stopped more than 90% of pancreatic cancer cell migration in lab tests.

Researchers tested a class of compounds called PCAIs against pancreatic cancer cells carrying KRAS mutations.

KRAS is one of cancer’s most difficult targets, and it drives many pancreatic tumors by keeping growth signals switched on.

One compound, NSL-YHJ-2-27, stood out. At a low dose, it blocked more than 90% of cancer-cell migration, a key step involved in invasion and metastasis.

It also reduced proteins that help cells move, disrupted the internal scaffolding cancer cells use to spread, and triggered cell death in 3D tumor-like spheroids.

Unexpectedly, the compound did not simply shut cancer signaling down. It pushed major growth pathways into overdrive, possibly overwhelming the cells with stress.

This is promising, but very early. It has not yet been tested in animals or humans.

📃 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Ofosu-Asante et al., “The anticancer effects of PCAIs in pancreatic cancer cells involve MAPK and PI3K/AKT pathways hyperactivation”, Oncotarget (2026)

Our trip to Glacier National Park with our dear friends Matt and Carrie Harris was amazing and just what Cindy and I needed.

It’s been seven weeks since Mom passed. We’re still adjusting to a new normal, and some days the emotional and physical exhaustion catches up with me. I’m not overwhelmed by grief every moment, but I rarely sleep through the night. I wake up three or four times, often without a dream or even a thought about Mom. I don’t know whether that’s part of grieving, me turning 60 in December or just a coincidence. Maybe time will tell.

This was our first big trip since she passed, and I’ll be honest, I sometimes felt guilty even planning it. Part of me wondered whether enjoying myself meant I wasn’t honoring her enough, or that I was moving on too quickly.

After a lot of prayer and reflection, I now know better. I will never “get over” losing Mom. But she wouldn’t want us to stop living, either. Because her health made travel difficult, she loved experiencing adventures through us. She always wanted pictures, and she couldn’t wait to hear every story when we got home. I believe she had an even better view of this trip from heaven.

Glacier did our souls good. We thought of Mom often, and out there in God’s country, we felt close to her. I’ll always cherish that.

A strong upper-level weather system will draw a surge of very humid air into the region following a morning round of rain. SHUT THE FRONT DOOR...AND OPEN THE WINDOWS! 

Ok, maybe not so much, but ALMOST! This could be our FIRST widespread sign around Florida that fall weather is on the way. 

Here is what you need to know:

1.) A weak front will pass through Tuesday night & Wednesday, switching the winds from the northeast. That should be enough to bring noticeably drier, less humid air down into North & Central Florida for Wednesday. The area most likely to feel it would be along & north of the I-4 corridor.      

2.) A few showers are possible as this front moves by, North Florida on Tuesday & Central Florida on Wed. AM. 

3.) Dew points will fall into the 60s. This is a modest humidity reduction. We'll be going from "swampy" to "moderately humid," so don't expect too much. 

4.) This isn't really a "cold" front for Florida. We may see some lows in the 60s Wed & Thu AM in the Panhandle, but for everyone else it's lows in the low 70s, which is just normal for this time of year. 

5.) The afternoon will still be warm to hot as dry air warms FAST, so expect upper 80s to the low to mid 90s Wed PM 🥵

6.) South Florida: Not participating. Sorry folks, this one is NOT going to reach you. 

Yes, this first front is not really much to get excited about, BUT it is a sign of the seasons finally showing a sign of change, even here in Florida.

TROPICS | SEPT 14, 2026 4 AM | NHC has increased the chance of a system developing in the Atlantic NE of the islands to 30% over the next 7 days. 

A weak wave will travel into a more favorable location for development this week & some tropical system formation here is possible later in the week.

There is a HUGE difference among the models with this system & it's a rather unusual one. The difference here is not EURO vs GFS; it's traditional vs AI. The traditional physics-based models are not doing much with a system in this region. They really don't have much, if anything, forming here. 

On the other hand, the AI models are going CRAZY, calling for tropical storm & maybe even hurricane development. The next name on the list is Fay.

The AI models have been a lot more bullish with systems this year overall. The AI ensembles show MANY more potential storm tracks vs. the traditional models. The indicators for this system from the AI models are the strongest we've seen in any system so far this year. 

The threat to the U.S. from this is VERY low. There will be a couple of cold fronts coming off the U.S. East Coast in the next 5-10 days. These fronts would keep this system out to sea; a fish storm. All the AI models turn this system north & northeast AWAY from the U.S. East Coast. 

For Florida, this storm would form too far north to be a threat.  

I'll keep you updated.

items.author: EdPiotrowskiWPDE
items.text:
BAD DAY IN WEATHER HISTORY

37 years ago today, Hurricane Hugo was intensifying and became a major hurricane (category 3) with 115 mph winds as it approached the Lesser Antilles. 18 hours later, it would become a category 5 with winds of 160 mph.

7 years ago, Hurricane Florence came ashore in southeast North Carolina then crawled across South Carolina dumping nearly 2 feet of rain. That sent rivers to levels that shattered records set by Hurricane Matthew in 2016.

Hugo was an example of the sheer destructive power of wind and surge.

Florence was an example of how catastrophic rain can be. Because of how painstakingly slow Hurricane Florence moved, unprecedented rainfall produced catastrophic flooding, especially on our rivers. Record river crests set by Matthew in 2016 were shattered by inches to over 3 ft with Hurricane Florence.

And to think, it was "just a tropical storm" that moved through our area. We had no hurricane-force winds.

Lesson here. The amount of rainfall from a tropical system isn't proportional to the strength of the system, it's proportional to the speed of the system. As mentioned, Florence was a tropical storm when it moved through our area yet it dumped nearly 24" of rain in spots. It was literally crawling at 3 mph. Hurricane Hugo was a category 4 hurricane that barreled across the Carolinas at over 25 mph. It only produced 2-8" of rain across the state.

items.author: secretsofuniverse
items.text:
Tinnitus is the perception of ringing, buzzing, clicking, or hissing when no external sound is present.

For many people, the problem is not only in the ears. The brain may become stuck treating phantom sound as important instead of filtering it into the background.

A new review suggests psilocybin, the psychedelic compound in magic mushrooms, could affect some of the same brain systems involved in tinnitus.

These include serotonin signaling, glutamate, GABA, and brain plasticity — the brain’s ability to reshape its connections.

A mouse study also suggests psilocybin can change how the brain filters repeated sounds.

But no clinical trial has shown that psilocybin safely treats tinnitus in humans.

For now, this is a research direction, not a therapy.

📃 REVIEW PAPER
📌 Lu et al., “Current status and future prospects of research on psilocybin's regulation of neurotransmitters and their receptors related to the pathogenesis of tinnitus”, Hearing Research (2026)
